prompt: What is a Git repository?
body: A repository is the project folder plus the hidden `.git` directory. The `.git` directory stores commits, branches, and history. A commit is a snapshot of the tracked files at a point in time, with a message and a link to its parent commit. Git stores snapshots, not a separate copy of every file on every commit.

hints.text: Look for the hidden .git directory.

prompt: What does a commit record?

options.text: A snapshot of tracked files with a message and parent
A full copy of the folder, including ignored files

explanation: A commit records the tracked snapshot, the message, and the parent link. Ignored files are not included.

prompt: Which command creates a new repository in the current folder?
explanation: `git init` creates the repository metadata. `git clone` copies an existing repository.

prompt: What does a commit capture at a point in time?
modelAnswer: A commit captures a snapshot of the tracked files, with a message and parent link.

hints.text: The answer is not the word diff.

prompt: Create a repository, make a commit, and inspect the log.

hints.text: Create a scratch folder first.

prompt: Working tree, staging area, and history
body: `git status` shows the state of the working tree and the staging area. `git diff` shows unstaged changes. `git diff --staged` shows changes that are already staged. `git add` moves changes from the working tree into the staging area. `git commit` records the staged snapshot.

hints.text: There are three places: working tree, index, and history.

prompt: Which command shows the state of the working tree and staging area?
explanation: `git status` reports working tree and staging state. `git log` shows commit history.

prompt: Which command shows unstaged changes?
explanation: `git diff` compares the working tree to the index. `git diff --staged` compares the index to the last commit.

prompt: Which command stages a file named notes.md?

hints.text: The command is two words.

prompt: What is a branch?
body: A branch is a movable pointer to a commit. Creating a branch does not copy the repository. `git switch -c feature` creates and switches to a new branch. Commits on that branch move the branch pointer forward. `git branch` lists branches, and `git switch main` changes the current branch.

hints.text: A branch is a label that moves.

prompt: Which command creates and switches to a branch named feature?
explanation: `git switch -c feature` creates and switches. `git branch feature` creates the branch but leaves you on the current branch.

prompt: What is a branch in Git?

options.text: A movable pointer to a commit
A full copy of the repository

explanation: Branches are lightweight pointers, not full copies.

prompt: Create a branch, commit on it, and switch back to main.

hints.text: Switch to main before you inspect the branches.

prompt: Merge feature into main.

steps.title: Switch to the target branch
steps.body: Run `git switch main`. The branch you are on is the branch that receives the merge.

steps.title: Inspect the result
steps.body: If Git fast-forwards, main moves to the feature commit. If histories diverged, Git may create a merge commit or stop on conflicts.

hints.text: The branch you switch to is the one that gets the merge.

checkpoint.prompt: Which branch receives the merge: the one you switch to, or the one you merge?

prompt: What does a fast-forward merge do?

options.text: Moves the target branch pointer forward without a merge commit

explanation: A fast-forward is possible when the target branch has no new commits. Git moves the pointer instead of creating a merge commit.

prompt: Which command merges feature into the current branch?
explanation: `git merge feature` merges feature into the branch you currently have checked out.

prompt: Which branch should you switch to before merging feature into main?
modelAnswer: Switch to `main`, then run `git merge feature`.

hints.text: The target branch is the one you check out.

prompt: Resolving a merge conflict
body: A conflict happens when both branches change the same part of a file. Git writes conflict markers: `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>`. Edit the file to the version you want, remove the markers, stage the resolved file with `git add`, then commit. Do not blindly delete the file or push the markers.

hints.text: The markers show both sides. You choose the final content.

prompt: Which markers show a merge conflict?
explanation: Git uses `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` to mark the two sides and the divider.

prompt: After resolving a conflict, what should you do?

options.text: Stage the resolved file and commit

explanation: Resolve the content, remove the markers, stage the file, then commit.

prompt: Create a conflict, resolve it, and finish the merge.

hints.text: Read both sides before you edit.

prompt: What is a remote?
body: A remote is a named URL for another copy of the repository. `origin` is the conventional name for the main remote. Add one with `git remote add origin <url>`. A remote is not a branch. `git remote -v` lists remotes and their URLs.

hints.text: origin is a name for a URL, not a branch.

check.prompt: What is `origin` a name for? (one word)

prompt: Which command adds a remote named origin?
explanation: `git remote add` registers a remote URL under a name.

prompt: What is origin?

options.text: A conventional name for a remote repository

explanation: `origin` is a remote name. The main branch is usually called `main`.

prompt: Add a local bare repository as a remote and push to it.

hints.text: A bare repository is a remote without a working tree.

prompt: Publish main to origin.

steps.title: Check the remote
steps.body: Run `git remote -v` and confirm origin points where you expect.

steps.title: Push and set upstream
steps.body: Run `git push -u origin main`. The `-u` records the upstream so later pushes can be shorter.

steps.title: Pull before you push next time
steps.body: If the remote has new commits, use `git pull` or `git fetch` and integrate before pushing.

hints.text: The first push often needs the upstream flag.

prompt: Which command pushes main and sets the upstream?
explanation: `git push -u origin main` uploads commits and records the upstream.

prompt: What does git pull do by default?

options.text: Fetches remote changes and merges them

explanation: `git pull` is fetch plus integration, usually a merge unless you configure rebase.

prompt: Which command downloads remote changes without merging them?
modelAnswer: `git fetch` downloads remote updates. It does not merge them into your branch.

hints.text: It is not git pull.

prompt: Push from one clone and pull into another using a local bare remote.

hints.text: Treat the bare repository as the shared server.

prompt: Pull requests on GitHub
body: A pull request asks to merge one branch into another. It shows the proposed diff, runs checks, and collects review. Reviewers can comment, request changes, or approve. A pull request does not deploy to production by itself. The merge happens after review and checks pass.

hints.text: A pull request is a review and merge request.

prompt: What does a pull request ask for?

options.text: Review and merge of one branch into another

explanation: A pull request proposes a merge and invites review. Deployment is a separate step.

prompt: What should happen before a pull request is merged?
explanation: Review and checks are the point of the pull request.

prompt: Explain the pull request flow to a new contributor.
modelAnswer: Create a branch, push it, open a pull request, respond to review and checks, then merge when approved.

hints.text: Name the branch, review, and merge steps.

prompt: Ignoring files
body: `.gitignore` keeps matching untracked files out of commits. It does not delete files from disk. If a file is already tracked, adding it to `.gitignore` does not stop tracking. Remove it from the index with `git rm --cached` and commit. Use `.gitignore` for secrets, build output, and local editor files.

hints.text: Ignoring and untracking are different.

prompt: What does .gitignore do?

options.text: Keeps matching untracked files out of commits

explanation: `.gitignore` affects tracking. It does not delete files.

prompt: A file is already tracked. You add it to .gitignore. What happens?

options.text: Git keeps tracking it until you remove it from the index

explanation: Ignore rules apply to untracked files. Use `git rm --cached` to untrack an existing file.

prompt: Keep a .env file out of a new repository and verify it is ignored.

hints.text: Check with git status after you create the ignore rule.

prompt: Undo and recovery
body: `git restore` changes the working tree. `git restore --staged` unstages without changing the file. `git revert` creates a new commit that reverses an earlier commit, which is safe on shared history. `git reset --hard` moves the branch and discards changes, so use it carefully. `git reflog` shows recent branch-tip movements and can help recover lost commits.

hints.text: Prefer revert on shared history.

prompt: Which command unstages a file while keeping the change?
explanation: `git restore --staged` unstages. `git reset --hard` discards changes and moves the branch.

prompt: Which command safely reverses a published commit by creating a new commit?
explanation: `git revert` creates a new commit that reverses the old one. It is safer on shared history.

prompt: Which command shows the history of branch-tip movements?
modelAnswer: `git reflog` shows recent branch-tip movements and can help recover commits.

hints.text: The word is short for reference log.

prompt: Restore a working-tree change and inspect the reflog.

hints.text: Do not use reset --hard for this exercise.
